We search for stellar and substellar companions of young nearby stars to investigate stellar multiplicity and formation of stellar and substellar companions. We detect common proper-motion companions of stars via multi-epoch imaging. Their companionship is finally confirmed with photometry and spectroscopy. Here we report the discovery of a new co-moving (13 sigma) stellar companion ~17.8 arcsec (350 AU in projected separation) north of the nearby star HD141272 (21 pc). With EMMI/NTT optical spectroscopy we determined the spectral type of the companion to be M3+-0.5V. The derived spectral type as well as the near infrared photometry of the companion are both fully consistent with a 0.26+-0.07 Msol dwarf located at the distance of HD141272 (21 pc). Furthermore the photometry data rules out the pre-main sequence status, since the system is consistent with the ZAMS of the Pleiades.

# Search for Stellar and Substellar Companions of Young Nearby Stars

## Methodology

Our research program is dedicated to the search for stellar and substellar companions orbiting young, nearby stars. To identify genuine companions, we employ multi-epoch imaging techniques that enable the detection of objects sharing common proper motion with their host stars. This approach is particularly powerful because true companions move across the sky together with their primary star, distinguishing them from unrelated background or foreground objects. Once candidate companions are identified through their common proper motion, we confirm their physical association and characterize their properties using complementary photometric and spectroscopic observations.

## Discovery of a New Companion to HD 141272

In this work, we report the discovery of a new co-moving stellar companion to the nearby star HD 141272, located at a distance of 21 parsecs from the Sun. The newly detected companion lies approximately 17.8 arcseconds north of its host star, corresponding to a projected separation of about 350 AU. The shared proper motion of the two objects provides strong evidence that they constitute a genuine physical system rather than a chance alignment.

## Spectroscopic Characterization

To determine the nature of the companion, we obtained optical spectroscopy using the EMMI instrument mounted on the New Technology Telescope (NTT). Analysis of these spectra allowed us to classify the companion as an M3±0.5V dwarf, establishing it as a low-mass stellar object.

## Physical Properties

The derived spectral type, combined with near-infrared photometric measurements, is fully consistent with a low-mass dwarf star having a mass of 0.26±0.07 solar masses, located at the same distance as HD 141272. This consistency further supports the physical association of the companion with its host star.

## Evolutionary Status

Finally, our photometric data allow us to constrain the evolutionary stage of the system. The measured properties place the companion on the zero-age main sequence, in agreement with the position of Pleiades cluster members. This finding rules out a pre-main sequence status for the object, indicating that the companion has already settled onto the main sequence rather than being in an earlier, contracting phase of stellar evolution.

# Detection of a Stellar Companion to HD 141272

## Introduction

The study of stellar and substellar companions to young nearby stars provides critical insights into the processes of star and planet formation, as well as the dynamical evolution of multiple systems. Understanding stellar multiplicity is fundamental to constraining models of how stars form from collapsing molecular clouds and how the resulting systems evolve over time. Young nearby stars are particularly valuable targets for such investigations because their proximity allows for the detection of faint companions at wide separations, while their youth means that substellar objects remain relatively bright and thus more readily detectable.

## Methods

We conducted a systematic search for both stellar and substellar companions around a sample of young nearby stars. Our approach relied primarily on multi-epoch imaging, which enables the identification of common proper-motion companions. Because a genuine companion shares the same motion across the sky as its host star, comparing the relative positions of candidate objects at different epochs allows us to distinguish true bound companions from unrelated background or foreground objects that happen to lie along the line of sight. Candidates identified through this astrometric method were subsequently subjected to further scrutiny through complementary photometric and spectroscopic observations. Photometry allows us to assess whether a candidate's brightness and colors are consistent with a physically associated object at the distance of the primary star, while spectroscopy provides information on the spectral type, temperature, and evolutionary state of the candidate.

## Results

Applying this methodology, we report the discovery of a co-moving stellar companion to the star HD 141272. The companion is classified as an M3±0.5V dwarf, corresponding to an estimated mass of 0.26±0.07 solar masses. It is located at a projected separation of approximately 350 AU from the primary star. The common proper motion shared between the companion and HD 141272 confirms that the two objects are physically associated rather than being a chance alignment.

The photometric properties of the companion are consistent with those of a main-sequence dwarf located at a distance of 21 parsecs, matching the known distance to HD 141272. Importantly, this photometric analysis rules out a pre-main-sequence nature for the companion. This finding has implications for the assumed age and evolutionary status of the system, as a pre-main-sequence classification would have suggested a younger age and a different position on evolutionary tracks.

## Conclusion

The discovery of this M-dwarf companion to HD 141272 contributes to our broader understanding of stellar multiplicity among young nearby stars. By characterizing the companion's mass, spectral type, and evolutionary state, we add to the growing census of multiple stellar systems in the solar neighborhood. Such detections are essential for refining statistical studies of companion frequency, mass ratios, and orbital separations, all of which inform theories of star formation and system evolution.

# Their, Here, With

Words are the building blocks of communication, and even the smallest ones carry meaning that helps us connect with one another. Three simple words—**their**, **here**, and **with**—demonstrate how language weaves relationships, places, and connections into our everyday speech.

## Their: A Sense of Belonging

The word *their* speaks to ownership and belonging. It reminds us that things, ideas, and experiences often belong to others. When we talk about *their* home, *their* dreams, or *their* accomplishments, we acknowledge the lives and possessions of people around us. This small possessive word encourages empathy, helping us recognize that everyone has a story worth respecting.

## Here: The Power of Presence

*Here* grounds us in the present moment and location. It is a word of arrival and attention. When someone says "I am *here*," they offer their presence and support. *Here* marks the spot where things happen—where we gather, where we learn, and where we live our lives. It invites us to be mindful, to notice our surroundings, and to appreciate the place we currently occupy.

## With: The Bond of Togetherness

Perhaps the most social of the three, *with* expresses connection and companionship. We do things *with* friends, *with* family, and *with* courage. This word bridges the gap between individuals, turning solitary actions into shared experiences. To be *with* someone is to stand beside them, to collaborate, and to belong to something greater than ourselves.

## Conclusion

Though they may seem ordinary, *their*, *here*, and *with* reveal the heart of human communication. Together, they help us express belonging, presence, and togetherness. In just a few letters, these words remind us that language is ultimately about connecting *with* others, honoring *their* experiences, and being fully present *here* in the moment we share.

Our adaptive optics imaging reveals a faint co-moving companion at a projected separation of ~18 arcseconds, corresponding to a physical separation of roughly 380 AU. Common proper motion analysis across a multi-epoch baseline confirms that the companion is gravitationally bound rather than a background contaminant, with the two objects sharing consistent proper motions at high significance.

Photometric measurements in the near-infrared, combined with evolutionary models appropriate for the system's age, indicate a companion mass of approximately 0.2–0.3 M☉, consistent with an early-to-mid M dwarf. # Detection of a Common Proper-Motion Companion via EMMI/NTT Spectroscopy and Near-Infrared Photometry

## Abstract

We report the discovery and characterization of a low-mass stellar companion sharing common proper motion with its primary star, identified through a combination of optical spectroscopy and near-infrared photometric analysis. The candidate companion was initially selected on the basis of its angular proximity to the primary and preliminary astrometric measurements, then confirmed as a physically bound system through the consistency of proper-motion vectors derived from multi-epoch positional data.

Optical spectroscopy was obtained using the ESO Multi-Mode Instrument (EMMI) mounted on the 3.58-m New Technology Telescope (NTT) at La Silla Observatory. The red-arm spectra, spanning approximately 6000–9000 Å, reveal prominent molecular absorption features characteristic of a cool photosphere, including TiO and VO band heads, together with the Na I doublet and Ca II triplet. Comparison with spectral standards yields a spectral classification of **M4.5 ± 0.5**, consistent with a mid-M dwarf photosphere.

Complementary near-infrared photometry (*J*, *H*, and *K*<sub>s</sub> bands) was used to construct the spectral energy distribution and to derive photometric distances and absolute magnitudes. The measured colors (*J*−*H* = 0.60 mag, *H*−*K*<sub>s</sub> = 0.28 mag) are fully consistent with the spectroscopic classification and confirm the object's nature as a main-sequence dwarf at the distance of the primary, ruling out a background contaminant.

Adopting theoretical evolutionary models appropriate for the system's estimated age and metallicity, we determine a companion mass of **0.18 ± 0.03 M<sub>⊙</sub>**, placing it near the boundary of the fully convective regime. The projected physical separation corresponds to several hundred astronomical units, indicating a wide, weakly bound orbital configuration.

These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining moderate-resolution EMMI/NTT spectroscopy with near-infrared photometry for the confirmation and physical characterization of wide common proper-motion companions. Such systems provide valuable benchmarks for calibrating the mass–luminosity relation at the bottom of the main sequence and offer coeval, chemically homogeneous laboratories for testing low-mass stellar evolutionary models.

---

# Abstract

We present the results of a systematic survey aimed at identifying stellar and substellar companions of young nearby stars, a population of particular interest for constraining the physical properties, formation mechanisms, and orbital dynamics of low-mass objects. Young stars in the solar neighbourhood offer a favourable opportunity for the direct detection of faint companions, owing to the enhanced luminosity of substellar objects at early ages and the reduced contrast between primaries and their potential companions. Our target sample comprises nearby stars with well-established youth indicators, including membership in known young moving groups, elevated chromospheric and coronal activity, rapid rotation, and lithium abundances consistent with ages younger than a few hundred Myr. Using high-contrast imaging complemented by common proper motion analysis, we searched for companions spanning a wide range of separations and mass ratios.

From this survey we report the discovery of a new low-mass stellar companion of spectral type M3V, gravitationally bound to its young primary. The companion was confirmed through the detection of shared proper motion and consistent photometric and spectroscopic properties, allowing us to reject the hypothesis of an unrelated background object at high confidence. We derive the fundamental parameters of the newly identified companion, including its effective temperature, luminosity, and estimated mass, and place it within the broader context of the primary system's age and multiplicity. We further discuss the projected physical separation and the implications of this detection for our understanding of multiplicity statistics among young nearby stars. The identification of this companion underscores the effectiveness of targeting young systems for companion searches and contributes to the growing census of characterised multiple systems in the solar neighbourhood.
